summary:
Tasmania stands under the Australian national framework, and its own layer adds protections beyond the federal floor. The Anti-Discrimination Act 1998 (Tas) prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity, gender expression, sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics, and was amended in September 2013 to extend protections to transgender and intersex people and to prohibit offending, humiliating, intimidating, insulting or ridiculing a person on the basis of actual or perceived gender, sexual orientation or gender identity. Tasmania is one of the Australian jurisdictions whose vilification law names gender identity as a protected ground.

Legal gender recognition in Tasmania is among the most permissive in Australia. The Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment Act 2019 received royal assent on 8 May 2019 and took effect on 5 September 2019, permitting self-declared gender registration on Tasmanian-registered births with no medical certificate or other medical document required. A person aged 16 or over may register male, female, indeterminate gender, non-binary or another self-described neither-entirely-male-nor-female gender by statutory declaration of identity and lived or seeking-to-live gender, subject to the Registrar's power to refuse terms outside the prescribed set. Parents or guardians may register a gender for children under 16, supported by the child's own gender declaration where able, or by statements of consistency with the child's will and preference with optional counselling evidence for those under 18. Birth sex registration remains male-or-female only and cannot be changed except to correct an initial error, but it ceases upon gender registration. The same reforms allow individuals to remove a gender descriptor entirely, allow parents to change the legal gender of their children, and extend the registration period for parents of intersex children to 120 days after birth. The 2019 legislation passed the House of Assembly on 10 April 2019 after Liberal Speaker Sue Hickey crossed the floor to vote with the Opposition, having already cleared the Legislative Council; the Tasmanian Government opposed the amendments and declined to rule out later repeal.

Historical offences carry an expungement and compensation regime. Cross-dressing was an offence under the Police Offences Act 1935 until its repeal in 2001, with Tasmania the only Australian state to have criminalised cross-dressing. Under the Expungement of Historical Offences Act 2017 (royal assent 21 November 2017), charges and convictions for cross-dressing offences under section 8(1)(d) of the Police Offences Act 1935 as in force before 12 April 2001, including attempts and inciting, instigating, aiding or abetting, are eligible for expungement on application to the Secretary, or by specified representatives where the person is deceased or lacks capacity. Eligibility for expungement took effect 9 April 2018, with compensation payments of up to $75,000 effective 2 August 2026, following a parliamentary apology on 13 April 2017.

Tasmania decriminalised consensual homosexual activity through the Criminal Code Amendment Act 1997, passed 1 May 1997, royal assent 13 May 1997, in force the following day, after penalties of up to 21 years that were the harshest in the Western world and after the United Nations Human Rights Committee decision in Toonen on 31 March 1994 and the federal Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994. Tasmania was the final Australian jurisdiction to do so, refusing to repeal after that federal act commenced on 19 December 1994 and acting only when faced with a likely High Court loss in Croome v Tasmania. The age of consent in Tasmania is 17 years, equal for all forms of sexual activity and shared only with South Australia.

A hate crimes bill that explicitly includes gender identity within the 1997 sentencing act passed the lower house in September 2025, with the upper house yet to vote. As of September 2026, conversion therapy practices remain legally permitted in Tasmania. No state-specific incident series or enforcement pattern of violence against trans people is documented in the sources held here.
tangentialFactors:
Tasmania's equality timeline is the longest-running in Australia: it was the last jurisdiction to decriminalise male homosexuality, in May 1997, and the only state to have criminalised cross-dressing, until 2001. Both categories of historic conviction are now expungable, with compensation available from August 2026.

Same-sex couples can enter registered domestic partnerships in Tasmania with an optional official ceremony, and equality of adoption rights for same-sex couples applied across all Australian states and territories from April 2018. These are relationship-recognition facts rather than trans-specific ones, but they bear on how a trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status would be treated locally.

The 2019 birth-certificate reforms were enacted against the sitting government's opposition, which had declined to rule out a future repeal. That political posture is unresolved: the reforms stand today, but the government's stated position is part of the record.

The federal discrimination backdrop, including the August 2024 Federal Court decision reported by Reuters against a female-only app, applies in Tasmania as everywhere in Australia; Tasmania's own Anti-Discrimination Act independently covers gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics.
localsOnly:
Residents benefit from the full scope of the Anti-Discrimination Act 1998 (Tas) as amended in September 2013, which reaches conduct that offends, humiliates, intimidates, insults or ridicules on the basis of actual or perceived gender, sexual orientation or gender identity, and which the 2019 amendments extended to gender expression, sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics, including as grounds for the prohibition on incitement of hatred.

Legal gender change for residents is governed by the 2019 amendments to the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act 1999, requiring only a simple statutory declaration with no forced divorce, sex reassignment surgery or other medical requirement. The age at which a person may change legal gender without parental permission is sixteen.

Historic convictions for cross-dressing before 2001 and for homosexual sexual offences before 1997 are expungable under the Expungement of Historical Offences Act 2017, with eligibility from 9 April 2018 and compensation of up to $75,000 effective 2 August 2026, following the parliamentary apology of 13 April 2017.

Conversion therapy practices remain legally permitted in Tasmania as of September 2026, a resident-facing gap in an otherwise protective statutory scheme.

The hate crimes bill adding gender identity to the 1997 sentencing act has cleared only the lower house; residents do not yet have that sentencing enhancement in force.
outOfScopeNotes:
No state-specific incident series or documented enforcement pattern of violence against trans people in Tasmania appears in the sources held here. The absence of such a series is unresolved rather than evidence of safety.

The status of the hate crimes bill after its September 2025 lower-house passage is unresolved: the sources do not record an upper-house vote or final outcome.

Whether the Tasmanian Government has moved to repeal or amend the 2019 birth-certificate reforms after opposing them at enactment is not sourced here.

The Queensland Human Rights Commission page announcing better discrimination protections for gender-diverse people was not retrievable (HTTP 403); it concerns another Australian jurisdiction and is carried as national-patchwork context only, not as a Tasmanian fact.
